## August 24, 1931

You turned 95 twelve days ago. To understand what that number actually means, consider where you started: in the pit of the Great Depression, with Adolf Hitler ascending in Germany, and the world order that had survived the first war already cracking toward the second.

---

**On the exact day you were born**, the British government collapsed and was instantly reconstituted. Ramsay MacDonald resigned as Labour Prime Minister that morning under crushing pressure from the global financial crisis — Britain was hemorrhaging gold reserves, facing a run on the pound, and unable to agree on how deeply to cut unemployment benefits. Within hours, King George V asked MacDonald to form a National Government, a cross-party emergency coalition. MacDonald accepted, was immediately expelled from his own Labour Party as a class traitor, and continued governing Britain with Conservative support. It was a moment that crystallized the political rupture the Great Depression was causing across democracies everywhere: normal politics had stopped working, and improvised emergency arrangements were taking their place.

**The world you entered was in genuine economic catastrophe.** The American stock market had crashed twenty-two months before your birth. By August 1931, unemployment in the United States was approaching 16 percent and still climbing — it would not peak until 1933, when one in four Americans who wanted work could not find it. Banks were failing in waves. The Dust Bowl was building across the Great Plains. The human misery embedded in the year of your birth is difficult to overstate: breadlines, foreclosures, families sleeping in parks, a political class that had no framework for what was happening and no tools adequate to fix it.

**The shadow of Hitler was already darkening the horizon.** In September 1930 — eleven months before your birth — the Nazi Party went from 12 seats in the German Reichstag to 107, becoming the second-largest party in Germany in a single election. By the time you were born, Hitler was not a fringe figure; he was the most dangerous politician in Europe. You were seventeen months old when he became Chancellor. You were not yet four when the Nuremberg Laws stripped German Jews of citizenship. The war those years were building toward would define your childhood and the lives of everyone around you.

**Twenty-five days after your birth**, on September 18, 1931, Japanese officers staged a fabricated incident near Mukden in Manchuria — blew up a small section of their own railway and blamed Chinese saboteurs — and used it as a pretext to invade. This was not yet the Second World War. But it was the first major act of the era of aggression that would become it. The League of Nations condemned Japan's invasion and did nothing. The lesson that aggression could proceed without consequence echoed forward through the decade.

---

**What the ninety-five years look like:**

You were eight years old when Germany invaded Poland. Old enough to understand that the world was at war; young enough that the adults in your life were trying to protect you from the worst of it, which meant you absorbed the war's weight through ration books and blackout curtains and the absence of older relatives. You were thirteen when it ended.

You came of age into the postwar boom — the most sustained period of broadly shared prosperity in American history. You were nineteen when the Korean War began. You watched television arrive as a household fixture, watched the interstate highway system get built, watched a country decide it had defeated catastrophe and deserved to enjoy itself.

You were twenty-eight when the first satellite orbited Earth, thirty-eight when men walked on the Moon. You were forty-two during Watergate. Fifty-eight when the Berlin Wall fell — old enough to grasp what it meant to people who had lived under that wall, because you remembered the world that built it.

You were seventy when September 11 happened. Eighty-nine during COVID. Ninety-five now, in the opening years of artificial intelligence as a mass phenomenon.

Here is one way to measure the distance: when you were born, there were Americans still alive who had fought in the Civil War. The last verified Union veteran, Albert Woolson, lived until 1956 — you were twenty-five. You were born close enough to the Civil War to share the planet with its soldiers. You now share the planet with systems that can write, reason, and generate images on command.

---

You entered a world in depression and drift, with the catastrophe of the 1930s and 1940s still ahead of it. You have outlasted the Depression, the war, the Cold War, and the post-Cold War order that was supposed to be the final arrangement. Whatever the world becomes next, you have already seen more of its transformations than almost anyone alive.
